name: Arthur Pembroke
presenting_complaint: Progressive confusion, drowsiness and dehydration over several days

medical_history.social: Lives alone in a retirement village. Reduced oral intake for several days with a recent 'flu-like' illness. Limited mobility.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought in after several days of increasing confusion, drowsiness and reduced intake following a viral illness. He is profoundly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes, a BGL of 41 mmol/L, tachycardia and mild hypotension, and is drowsy (GCS 13). There is minimal ketosis. This is hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS), not DKA. Obs: BP 104/62, HR 112, RR 20, SpO2 95%, Temp 37.6 C, GCS 13, BGL 41 mmol/L.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Distinguish HHS from DKA: older type 2 patient, symptoms over DAYS, very high glucose, marked dehydration, high osmolality, little/no ketosis or acidosis, often confused
Duration of polyuria, polydipsia, reduced oral intake and progressive confusion/drowsiness
Identify the PRECIPITANT: infection (recent viral illness), silent MI, stroke, medications (steroids, diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors), non-adherence, dehydration
Review usual diabetic therapy and adherence (metformin, gliclazide); note CKD and ACE inhibitor
Symptom screen for focal deficit, chest pain, sepsis source; document medications and allergies
objective: Calculate effective serum osmolality [2 x Na + glucose] and blood glucose; expect osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
Bloods: venous blood gas (pH usually >7.3, bicarbonate >15 = minimal acidosis), UEC (Na, K, urea, creatinine), FBC, glucose, ketones (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate low), CMP, CRP
Septic/precipitant screen: blood and urine cultures, CXR, urinalysis; 12-lead ECG and troponin to exclude silent MI/arrhythmia
Assess hydration and haemodynamics: BP, HR, capillary refill, mucous membranes, urine output (insert urinary catheter to monitor output), conscious level
Continuous cardiac and neuro monitoring; hourly BGL and regular electrolytes to track corrected sodium and correction RATE
assessment: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) — profound hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration with minimal ketosis, in an elderly type 2 diabetic
Precipitated by intercurrent infection/dehydration; exclude sepsis, silent MI and stroke
High risk of thromboembolism (VTE) due to hyperviscosity and immobility
Acute-on-chronic kidney injury from severe volume depletion; risk of cerebral oedema/osmotic demyelination if corrected too rapidly
plan: FLUIDS FIRST and cautiously — fluids do most of the work and are given more slowly than in DKA: IV 0.9% sodium chloride, typically 0.5-1 L over the first hour then titrate to gradual rehydration over 24-48 h guided by osmolality and haemodynamics
Aim to lower glucose gradually (target fall roughly 4-6 mmol/L per hour) and limit sodium/osmolality correction to a slow rate to avoid cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis
Delay insulin until fluids have started; only add a LOW-rate fixed insulin infusion (approximately 0.05 units/kg/hour) if glucose is not falling adequately with fluids alone
Potassium replacement guided by levels: add KCl to fluids once K is below ~5.0-5.5 mmol/L and the patient is passing urine; withhold insulin if K <3.5 until replaced
VTE prophylaxis with prophylactic-dose LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin) given the high thrombotic risk, unless contraindicated
Treat the precipitant: empirical antibiotics for infection after cultures; withhold metformin (AKI/lactic acidosis risk) and review nephrotoxic/hypoglycaemic agents
Add 5% glucose-containing fluid alongside saline once BGL approaches ~14-15 mmol/L to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia
Escalate to ICU/HDU and endocrinology; hourly BGL, regular UEC/osmolality, strict fluid balance and neuro obs

critical_errors: Treating HHS like DKA and correcting glucose, sodium or osmolality too rapidly — risks cerebral oedema and central pontine myelinolysis
Giving aggressive early insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation (causes rapid osmotic/fluid shifts and cardiovascular collapse)
Continuing metformin despite AKI/severe dehydration (lactic acidosis risk)
must_not_miss: Fluids first, slow and careful correction (fluids do most of the work)
Potassium monitored and replaced; insulin started only at a low rate after fluids
